title: Homework 2: k Sample Inference
text:
Code
set.seed(354)

R <- 1000
simulations <- vector("list", R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  simulations[[i]] <- data.frame(
    value = rnorm(150, mean = 0, sd = 1),
    group = factor(rep(1:5, each = 30))
  )
}







Code
error_unadjusted <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  test_unadjusted <- pairwise.t.test(
    dat$value, dat$group,
    p.adjust.method = "none"
  )

  error_unadjusted[i] <- any(
    test_unadjusted$p.value < 0.05,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}

mean(error_unadjusted)


[1] 0.294


At least one pairwise comparison provided statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean difference in 294 of the 1,000 simulations (p < 0.05). These are Type I errors, giving an estimated family-wise error rate of 29.4%.





Code
error_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  fit <- aov(value ~ group, data = dat)
  test_tukey <- rstatix::tukey_hsd(fit)

  error_tukey[i] <- any(test_tukey$p.adj < 0.05)
}

mean(error_tukey)


[1] 0.053


After Tukey’s HSD adjustment, at least one pairwise comparison provided statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean difference in 53 of the 1,000 simulations (adjusted p < 0.05). Since all population means were zero, these are Type I errors, and the estimated family-wise error rate is 5.3%.






Code
error_bh <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  test_bh <- pairwise.t.test(
    dat$value, dat$group,
    p.adjust.method = "BH"
  )

  error_bh[i] <- any(
    test_bh$p.value < 0.05,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}

mean(error_bh)


[1] 0.047


After BH adjustment, at least one pairwise comparison provided statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean difference in 47 of the 1,000 simulations, giving an estimated family-wise error rate of 4.7%. This was much lower than the unadjusted rate of 29.4% and close to Tukey’s rate of 5.3%.
BH targets the false discovery rate (FDR), whereas Tukey’s HSD controls the family-wise error rate (FWER).

title: Homework 2: k Sample Inference
text:
2 Question 2

2.1 Part a


Code
# Required sample size per group
pwr::pwr.anova.test(
  k = 5,
  f = 0.25,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)



     Balanced one-way analysis of variance power calculation 

              k = 5
              n = 39.1534
              f = 0.25
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8

NOTE: n is number in each group


Code
# Power curve
n <- 2:100

power <- sapply(n, function(x) {
  pwr::pwr.anova.test(
    k = 5, n = x, f = 0.25, sig.level = 0.05
  )$power
})

plot(n, power, type = "l",
     xlab = "Sample size per group",
     ylab = "Power",
     main = "ANOVA Power Curve")

abline(h = 0.80, col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = 40, col = "blue", lty = 2)









The required sample size is roughly 40 participants per group and 200 in total. The graph shows that 40 participants per group achieves slightly more than 80% power.
Since every group in the original groups had more than 40 participants, the study is powered for the overall ANOVA under the assumed moderate effect size. This calculation assumes equal group sizes, so it does not provide the exact power of the original unequal-sized design.


2.2 Part b


Code
# Non-centrality parameter and power
lambda <- 150 * 0.25^2
lambda


[1] 9.375


Code
critical <- qf(0.95, 4, 145)
pf(critical, 4, 145, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)


[1] 0.6675964


Code
# Alternative F distribution
curve(df(x, 4, 145, ncp = lambda), from = 0, to = 10,
      xlab = "F", ylab = "Density",
      main = "Alternative F Distribution: N = 150")
abline(v = critical, col = "red", lty = 2)









With 30 participants per group, the non-centrality parameter is 9.375 and the power is approximately 66.8%. Therefore, N = 150 is insufficient to achieve the desired 80% power.


2.3 Part c


Code
# Power for different sample sizes per group
n <- 40:500

power_c <- sapply(n, function(x) {
  PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test(
    n = x,
    groups = 5,
    delta = 0.25,
    within.var = 0.7152,
    sig.level = 0.05
  )$power
})

# Power with 40 participants per group
power_c[1]


[1] 0.07866837


Code
# Smallest sample size achieving at least 80% power
n_required <- min(n[power_c >= 0.80])
n_required


[1] 293


An overall ANOVA can detect differences among groups having different means. However, detecting the smaller difference between stages 1 and 2 is harder, especially after Tukey’s adjustment for multiple comparisons.
With 40 participants per group, the power is only about 7.9%. Using the pooled variance of 0.7152, approximately 293 participants per group are needed to achieve 80% power for this comparison.


2.4 Part d


Code
library(Superpower)

for (n in c(40, 80)) {

  design <- ANOVA_design(
    design = "5b",
    n = n,
    mu = c(2.92, 3.11, 3.36, 4.04, 4.35),
    sd = sqrt(0.80),
    plot = FALSE
  )

  result <- ANOVA_power(
    design,
    nsims = 1000,
    seed = 354,
    emm = TRUE,
    emm_p_adjust = "tukey",
    verbose = FALSE
  )

  print(paste("Sample size per group:", n))
  print(result$main_result)
  print(result$emm_results)
}

title: Homework 2: k Sample Inference
text:
3 Question 3

3.1 Part a
Let \(\mu_{2C}\), \(\mu_{6C}\), \(\mu_{16C}\), and \(\mu_{16T}\) denote the population mean SUVmax values for the 2-month control, 6-month control, 16-month control, and 16-month treatment groups, respectively.
\[
H_0: \mu_{2C} = \mu_{6C} = \mu_{16C} = \mu_{16T}
\]
\[
H_a: \text{At least one population mean differs.}
\]


3.2 Part b


Code
dat3 <- data.frame(
  SUVmax = c(
    1.48969, 1.30168, 1.30620,
    4.36000, 4.28807, 3.64184,
    7.30182, 7.12416, 8.28764,
    4.69304, 2.51326, 2.38019
  ),
  group = factor(
    rep(c("2M Control", "6M Control",
          "16M Control", "16M Treatment"), each = 3),
    levels = c("2M Control", "6M Control",
               "16M Control", "16M Treatment")
  )
)

# Means and standard deviations
aggregate(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3, FUN = mean)


          group   SUVmax
1    2M Control 1.365857
2    6M Control 4.096637
3   16M Control 7.571207
4 16M Treatment 3.195497


Code
aggregate(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3, FUN = sd)


          group    SUVmax
1    2M Control 0.1072666
2    6M Control 0.3955041
3   16M Control 0.6267761
4 16M Treatment 1.2986162


Code
# Display all observations
stripchart(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3,
           vertical = TRUE, method = "stack", pch = 19,
           xlab = "Group", ylab = "Heart SUVmax",
           main = "Heart SUVmax by Age and Treatment",
           cex.axis = 0.8)









Among the control groups, mean heart SUVmax increased with age (approximately 1.37, 4.10, and 7.57 for 2, 6, and 16 months, respectively). The 16-month treatment group had a lower mean (approximately 3.20) than the 16-month control group, placing it between the two younger control groups.


3.3 Part c


Code
test3 <- oneway.test(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3)
test3



    One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)

data:  SUVmax and group
F = 98.464, num df = 3.0000, denom df = 3.5496, p-value = 0.0006851


SUVmax is quantitative. The sample standard deviations differ substantially across groups, so I used Welch’s ANOVA because it does not assume equal population variances. The rats are not connected in certain ways so I assume independence. The observations per group are three, which is low, so the results should be interpreted cautiously.
Welch’s ANOVA gives \(F = 98.46\), with 3 and 3.55 degrees of freedom (p = 6.85^{-4}). Since p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The data provide statistically discernible support that at least one population mean heart SUVmax differs among the four groups.


3.4 Part d


Code
posthoc3 <- rstatix::games_howell_test(
  dat3, SUVmax ~ group
)

posthoc3


# A tibble: 6 × 8
  .y.    group1      group2     estimate conf.low conf.high   p.adj p.adj.signif
* <chr>  <chr>       <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>       
1 SUVmax 2M Control  6M Control    2.73      1.31     4.15  0.0119  *           
2 SUVmax 2M Control  16M Contr…    6.21      3.81     8.60  0.00720 **          
3 SUVmax 2M Control  16M Treat…    1.83     -3.30     6.96  0.308   ns          
4 SUVmax 6M Control  16M Contr…    3.47      1.56     5.39  0.00801 **          
5 SUVmax 6M Control  16M Treat…   -0.901    -5.47     3.67  0.698   ns          
6 SUVmax 16M Control 16M Treat…   -4.38     -8.51    -0.244 0.0431  *           


Games–Howell comparisons showed statistically discernible increases in mean heart SUVmax across the control groups: 2 versus 6 months (adjusted p = 0.0119), 2 versus 16 months (p = 0.0072), and 6 versus 16 months (p = 0.00801). The 16-month treatment group had a lower mean than the 16-month control group (estimated difference = −4.38, adjusted p = 0.0431), supporting a reduction associated with low-dose nicotine.
The treatment group did not differ significantly from the 2-month or 6-month control groups (adjusted p = 0.308 and 0.698, respectively), but these results do not establish equivalence to younger mice.


3.5 Part e
The results support the hypothesis that SUVmax increases with age and is reduced by low-dose nicotine in older mice. All three control groups differed significantly, with higher mean SUVmax at older ages. Although the treatment group did not differ significantly from the younger controls, this does not establish that treatment restored SUVmax to younger levels.

AI Use Statement
I believe generative AI can be a useful tool for learning when it supports rather than replaces my own thinking. I would use AI to help explain unfamiliar concepts, troubleshoot code, and identify possible mistakes in my work. However, I do not think AI should replace my own statistical reasoning or analysis. I should be able to understand and explain the work that I submit. I also think it is important to use AI critically and transparently. AI can provide incorrect or biased information, so I am responsible for checking its responses rather than accepting them automatically. This approach reflects the ASA’s emphasis on accountability, transparency, and integrity in statistical practice (Cipolli 2026; American Statistical Association 2022).

title: Homework 1: One-Sample Inference
text:
The data are the proportions of successful retrievals out of 12 tests for each dog, so they are quantitative rather than simple 0/1 Bernoulli trials. Thus, a one-sample z-test is not a good fit.
A one-sample t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test are plausible.
For the one-sample t-test, the population does not appear to be approximately Gaussian, since there are quite a few observations at the upper bound of 1 and the data are clearly left-skewed. The sample size (\(n = 10\)) is not large enough to rely on the CLT either. For the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the data do not appear symmetric for the same reason stated above. The sample size is not large enough for the asymptotic approximation either.
One noticable thing is that quite a few observations have the same value, which introduces ties if the Wilcoxon test is applied. Furthermore, there are several zeros in the second data set (paired difference), which complicates the ranking process. Thus, I might choose to use the one-sample t-test.





Statistical Questions:

Whether the dogs were better than chance, which we assume is 50%, at returning the new objects when requested.
Whether there was a difference in the dogs’ retrieval performance between the direct and overhearing conditions.

Researchers observed (n = 10) dogs and recorded the proportion of successful retrievals out of 12 tests for each dog. The observed proportions were
\(\{1.0000,\ 1.0000,\ 0.7500,\ 1.0000,\ 0.4167,\ 0.8333,\ 0.7500,\ 0.8333,\ 0.8333,\ 1.0000\}\)
They also considered the paired differences (direct − overhearing):
\(\{-0.0833,\ 0.0000,\ -0.0833,\ -0.0833,\ 0.5833,\ 0.0833,\ -0.2500,\ 0.1667,\ 0.0000,\ -0.4167\}\)



We want to test if the dogs were better than chance, so we use right sided test:
\(H_0: \mu_X = 0.50\)
\(H_a: \mu_X > 0.50\)
where \(\mu_X\) is the population mean proportion of successful retrievals.




The variable of interest in quantitative.
The sample is probably representative of the larger population.
The sample observations are independent.
The underlying population distribution is not approximately Gaussian, since the observed data arae left-skewed and have several observations at the upper bound of 1. In addition, the sample size (\(n = 10\)) is too small to use CLT.




The one-sample t-test was performed using the following R code:


Code
x <- c(1.0000, 1.0000, 0.7500, 1.0000, 0.4167,
       0.8333, 0.7500, 0.8333, 0.8333, 1.0000)

t.test(x, mu = 0.50, alternative = "greater")



    One Sample t-test

data:  x
t = 5.9386, df = 9, p-value = 0.0001092
alternative hypothesis: true mean is greater than 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.736198      Inf
sample estimates:
mean of x 
  0.84166 


The test statistic is calculated as
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}.
\] The sample mean was \(\bar{x} = 0.8417\). The test resulted in \(t = 5.9386\) with \(df = 9\) and a one-sided p-value of \(0.0001092\).



We use a right-tailed test (\(\mu_X > \mu_0\)).

Observations of t that are substantially larger than 0.5, which correspond to observations of \(\bar{x}\) that are substantially larger than \(\mu_0\).
\(p\text{-value} = P(T \geq t) = P(T \geq 5.9386) = 0.0001092\)




We use the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\). Since the \(p\text{-value} = 0.0001092\) is less than \(0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis. The data provide statistically discernible support for the alternative hypothesis.
The test statistic \(t = 5.9386\) indicates that the observed sample mean is approximately 5.94 standard errors above the null hypothesized mean of \(0.50\). Therefore, the data suggest that the dogs’ mean retrieval performance is better than chance.



To evaluate the magnitude of the effect, Hedges’\(g\) was calculated.


Code
library(effectsize)

test.result <- t.test(x, mu = 0.50, alternative = "greater")

hedges_g(test.result)


Hedges' g |      95% CI
-----------------------
1.72      | [0.88, Inf]

- Deviation from a difference of 0.5.
- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [Inf].


The estimated effect size was Hedges’\(g = 1.72\), indicating a large effect. The mean retrieval performance was approximately 1.72 standard deviations above the chance level of \(0.50\).



The 95% confidence interval was obtained from the t-test result:


Code
test.result$conf.int


[1] 0.736198      Inf
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


We are 95% confident that the population mean retrieval proportion is approximately \([0.736, \infty)\). Since this lower bound is above the chance level of \(0.50\), the confidence interval is consistent with the conclusion that the dogs performed better than chance.

title: Homework 1: One-Sample Inference
text:
2 Question 2

2.1 Part a
The data a qualitative, and each trial is a Bournulli trial (either succeed or fail), so binomial distribution is possible. However, the trials may not be independent, since there should be correlations between each trials. Specifically, the performance of each dog in the two new-toy trials may tend to be consistent. Moreover, the probability of selecting the new toy by chance may not be exactly 50%, depending on dogs’ behaviors.


2.2 Part b
The probability that a dog succeed in both trials are
\[
p = (0.50)(0.50) = 0.25.
\]
Let \(X_i = 1\) be the dog \(i\) getting both toys right on the first try, and \(X_i = 0\) be otherwise,
\[
X_i \sim \operatorname{Bornoulli}(0.25).
\]
Therefore, the total number of dogs getting both toys right follows a binomial distribution.
\[
B \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(10, 0.25).
\]
Since all 10 dogs got both trials right,
\[
P(B=10) = \binom{10}{10}(0.25)^{10}(0.75)^0=(0.25)^{10} \approx 9.54 \times 10^{-7}.
\]
Thus, the probability that all \(n=10\) dogs would get both trials correct is approximately \(9.54 \times 10^{-7}\).


2.3 Part c
The Gaussian approximation has mean
\[
\mu_Y = np = 10(0.25) = 2.5
\]
and standard deviation
\[
\sigma_Y = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{10(0.25)(0.75)}
\approx 1.369.
\]
Using the continuity correction,
\[
P(B=10)
\approx
P(9.5 < Y < 10.5).
\]
And then we standardize it using
\[
Z = \frac{Y-\mu_Y}{\sigma_Y}.
\]
The lower and upper bounds are
\[
\begin{aligned}
z_{\text{lower}} &= \frac{9.5-2.5}{1.369}
\approx 5.11, \\
z_{\text{upper}} &= \frac{10.5-2.5}{1.369}
\approx 5.84
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
P(B=10)
\approx
P(5.11 < Z < 5.84)
\approx 1.57 \times 10^{-7}.
\]
Compared to \(9.54 \times 10^{-7}\), which is the binomial probability from Part b, the Gaussian probability is much smaller. They are not close.
This is because one of the conditions to apply Gaussian distribution to approximate probabilities, is to make sure that
\[
np \ge 15,\\
and \\
n(1-p) \ge 15.
\]
In this case,
\[
np = 10(0.25) = 2.5\\
and \\
n(1-p) = 10(1-0.25) = 7.5,
\] both of which are less than 15, so the Gaussian approximation conditions are not satisfied.


2.4 Part d
No, it doesn’t make sense to make inference using the Gaussian method.
Given that all 10 dogs are successful, or \(\hat p = 1\), the standard error of the sample would be 0, as calculated below:
\[
SE = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
= \sqrt{\frac{1(0)}{10}} = 0.
\]
When we try to estimate \(Z = \frac{estimate - null value}{SE}\), the denominator would become zero, which is undefined. It would be hard to estimate confidence interval too.
